title: Striped Bass Are in Trouble, and Anglers Are Worried
summary:
Bill Jakob has fished for striped bass for more than 60 years. Near Montauk, New York, he once caught eight or nine fish up to 40 pounds. Now he and many East Coast anglers worry because the fish are not showing up as often, and young fish are harder to find.

Scientists agree. Regulators said last week the fish have had eight years of poor reproduction in Chesapeake Bay. Heavy fishing is only part of the problem; warming water, low river flow, drought, pollution, and possibly more seals and sharks may make recovery harder.

Up to 90 percent spawn and grow there. They do best in cool, wet springs, but since 2019 low flows and high temperatures have meant fewer young fish.

Striped bass are prized from Maine to Florida. Industry members say fishing adds about $8 billion and as many as 100,000 jobs. Regulators have not cut recreational catch levels, but some fishermen say a temporary pause like one in the 1980s may be needed. Experts and anglers agree the fish are not replacing themselves fast enough.
why_it_matters: If striped bass keep becoming harder to find, a child's fishing trip with family could end with far fewer fish to catch and enjoy.

background_read: Striped bass are fish that live along the East Coast and spawn in Chesapeake Bay, where many of their young grow up.
They do best in cool, wet springs, when river water helps young fish survive and grow.
When the water gets warmer, river flow drops, and fishing stays heavy, fewer young fish are born, so the fish cannot replace themselves fast enough.
